days.title: Platforms and reusable assets
days.intro: What a platform is and why teams build internal developer platforms, then the reusable assets a platform offers. Most of the weight is **Domain-Driven Design**: bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, aggregates and domain events, which the instructor flagged for the written exam.

topics.title: Introduction to Platforms
topics.overview: A platform provides shared services and interfaces on which applications and complementary products are built. This topic connects the internal developer platform (IDP), its architecture and adoption journey to platform thinking: enabling interactions between producers and consumers. Practise explaining both the developer experience and the engineering work behind a platform business.

topics.title: Reusable Assets and Frameworks
topics.overview: Platforms offer reusable services, frameworks and shared libraries. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) helps find cohesive service boundaries through bounded contexts and ubiquitous language, then shapes their internals with aggregates and domain events. The Scrum and Maid2Order cases apply these ideas; the final sections explain framework design and the coupling risks of shared libraries.

days.title: API design and services
days.intro: How services expose and share capability. API design covers REST, resources and HTTP methods, maturity, versioning and security. Reusable services then applies DDD to integration: context mapping between bounded contexts, aggregates as transaction boundaries, domain events, and the API gateway in front.

topics.title: API Design
topics.overview: This topic covers how to design, version, secure and operate APIs well. It starts with treating APIs as products and the design principles behind them, then covers REST constraints, resource and HTTP method best practices, the Richardson Maturity Model and GraphQL as an alternative. It moves on to versioning, OAuth-based security, resilience and testing, and distributed transactions across microservices. For the exam, expect to design or critique an API for a scenario and justify style, versioning and security choices.

topics.title: Reusable Services and API Gateway
topics.overview: Reusable services need explicit boundaries and deliberate integration. Context mappings describe relationships between bounded contexts; aggregates protect local invariants; domain events carry changes to other aggregates or services. This topic applies those ideas to car rental, compares orchestration with choreography, then explains gateway discovery and client SDKs.

days.title: Platform management and data
days.intro: Running the platform: service discovery, deployment strategies (rolling, blue-green, canary), circuit breakers, tracing, sagas, metrics and logs. The short case study applies them to a breaking database change. Data management then covers replication, sharding, caching, CAP and choosing a data model.

topics.title: Platform Management
topics.overview: Platform management keeps interactions scalable, available and safe to change. This topic covers discovery, deployment strategies, circuit breakers, rate limits, tracing, sagas, metrics and centralised logs. Practise choosing a tool from the failure it prevents and explaining the assumptions behind its guarantees.

topics.title: Deployment Case Study: Splitting the Payment Table
topics.overview: This case splits Payment into ChequePayment and ApplePayPayment without a single disruptive cutover. Follow the lecture’s four stages: add tables, release code that reads both layouts, backfill historical data, then switch reads. The key reasoning is data compatibility: reducing live exposure with a canary does not itself preserve every rollback path.

topics.title: Data Management
topics.overview: Choose datastores from the workload: required queries, write volume, consistency, availability, latency and schema evolution. This topic compares replication, sharding and caching, explains CAP during network partitions, then surveys key-value, document, wide-column, search, graph and SQL-over-files models. Treat named products as lecture examples rather than guarantees of every deployment.
